entries.title: Voice Interface for My Second Brain
entries.description: A voice-driven interface that turns natural speech into structured tasks, projects, events, and notes inside a customized Obsidian knowledge system.
problem: My Obsidian system already organized projects, tasks, events, notes, and daily information—but adding something still required opening the application, navigating to the right place, and entering the correct metadata.
I wanted the system to understand intent without requiring the interface.
solution: I built a voice layer that accepts natural speech, transcribes it, identifies the user's intent, and converts it into structured Markdown.
The system determines whether the input is a task, event, project, note, or other supported object and applies the appropriate metadata, template, folder, and date information.
The resulting item appears inside the existing Obsidian system without requiring manual organization.
howItWorks: **Example:** Spoken input — "Add Toyota interview Tuesday at 9 AM." The system identifies the event, extracts the date and time, generates the structured entry, and places it into the appropriate workflow.

entries.title: Multilingual Collaboration System
entries.description: A shared workspace where English and Japanese users can work on the same content in their own languages while changes remain synchronized.
problem: Traditional translation workflows create separate copies of the same information.
When one side edits the English version, the Japanese version can quickly become outdated—and vice versa. That creates duplicated work and makes multilingual collaboration difficult.
solution: I built a multilingual collaboration system where English and Japanese users interact with the same underlying content while viewing and editing it in their preferred language.
Changes are synchronized so the system behaves like one shared workspace rather than two translated documents.
The goal was not simply translation. It was designing collaboration around the reality that participants may not share the same language.

entries.title: Your Second Brain, Always Visible
entries.description: A calm, always-on interface that turns information from my Obsidian knowledge system into glanceable screens for tasks, projects, events, notes, and daily context.
problem: My tasks, calendar, projects, notes, and other useful information already existed digitally—but seeing them meant opening an application and actively looking for them.
I wanted important information to remain visible without another screen demanding attention.
solution: I connected my Obsidian knowledge system to an e-ink display.
A custom service reads structured Markdown and other data sources, determines what should be displayed, renders display-ready screens, and sends them to the device.
Different views can surface tasks, calendar information, projects, notes, highlights, meal planning, and other context.
howItWorks: **Design principle:** Inform, don't interrupt. The display is intentionally quiet. It provides ambient awareness without notifications, app switching, or another bright screen.

entries.title: Local-AI Document Pipeline
entries.description: A document-processing workflow that turns captured paperwork into organized knowledge, extracting tasks, deadlines, metadata, and useful information automatically.
problem: Important information arrives through paperwork, screenshots, PDFs, receipts, forms, and other documents.
Capturing the document is easy. Turning it into something searchable and actionable is not.
solution: I built a workflow connecting mobile document capture with a local AI processing system and desktop knowledge base.
Documents are processed, classified, and converted into structured information.
The pipeline can identify useful metadata, extract tasks and deadlines, assign tags, and route the resulting Markdown into the appropriate location in the knowledge system.
howItWorks: **Workflow:** Capture → OCR / extraction → classification → structured data → tasks / deadlines → Markdown → knowledge base

entries.title: Comic-to-Video Production Tool
entries.tagline: Creative Technology · Timeline UI · Keyframes · Automation
entries.description: A production interface for turning layered comic artwork into motion content using timeline editing, camera keyframes, and repeatable batch workflows.
problem: Turning static comic artwork into video requires repetitive editing: positioning artwork, creating camera movement, timing scenes, and repeating the process across many panels.
General-purpose video editors can do this, but the workflow is unnecessarily manual for comic-based content.
solution: I developed a purpose-built production tool for converting layered comic artwork into video.
The interface provides timeline editing, camera keyframes, layered asset control, and repeatable workflows designed specifically around comic production.

entries.title: Deterministic Comic Coloring Engine
entries.description: Consistent comic coloring without relying on generative output.
problem: Generative image workflows can produce inconsistent colors, character details, and visual styles across sequential comic panels.
That inconsistency breaks continuity across a page or issue, and makes generative coloring unreliable for production use.
solution: I'm building a deterministic processing system focused on preserving line art, repeatable color application, and style consistency across panels—supplemented by AI only where it doesn't compromise repeatability.
The engineering focus is on the pipeline itself: how line art is preserved, how color decisions are made deterministically, and how the same input reliably produces the same output.

entries.title: Proxy Priority — Intelligent Task Prioritization
entries.description: A task-prioritization system designed around what deserves attention now.
problem: Traditional task managers are good at storing tasks but often leave the harder question unanswered: what should I actually work on next?
As projects, deadlines, responsibilities, and priorities multiply, a flat task list becomes increasingly difficult to manage.
solution: I developed Proxy Priority as a structured approach to prioritization inside my broader productivity system.
Rather than relying only on manually ordered lists, the system provides additional structure for evaluating and surfacing work based on its current importance.

Proxy Priority is also integrated into my TRMNL e-ink dashboard pipeline (see Obsidian → TRMNL E-Ink Pipeline), so critical projects and tasks stay visible on an always-on display without opening Obsidian at all.

entries.title: 34-Site Deployment System
entries.description: A deployment system that lets me manage dozens of independent project websites without manually configuring hosting, DNS, repositories, and deployments for each one.
problem: Maintaining dozens of small project and portfolio sites creates repetitive infrastructure work.
Every new site normally requires repository setup, deployment configuration, DNS records, subdomains, and ongoing maintenance.
solution: I automated the workflow.
The system builds, exports, deploys, and manages 34 independent websites across GitHub and Cloudflare.
Each project remains independently version-controlled and mapped to its own subdomain while shared automation handles repetitive deployment work.

entries.title: PARA+NET Knowledge System
entries.tagline: Knowledge Management · Obsidian · Information Architecture · Automation
entries.description: Projects, Areas, Resources, Notes, Events, and Tasks connected in one system.
problem: PARA provides a useful structure for Projects, Areas, Resources, and Archives, but much of my daily information doesn't fit neatly into those categories.
Notes, events, and tasks are not secondary information. They are fundamental objects that connect everything else.
solution: I expanded the model into PARA+NET, adding Notes, Events, and Tasks as first-class parts of the system.
I then customized Obsidian and supporting workflows so these different objects could connect rather than live in isolated folders or applications.
The project combines information architecture, workflow design, metadata, interface customization, and automation.

entries.title: Social Card Studio
entries.description: A focused tool for producing consistent social graphics quickly.
solution: Repeatedly creating similar social graphics in general-purpose design software adds unnecessary setup and formatting work. I built a focused interface around the specific elements needed for social cards, reducing repetitive design work while maintaining visual consistency.

entries.title: Ka-Blam Formatter
entries.description: Automates repetitive formatting work for print publishing.
solution: Print production involves exact formatting requirements and repetitive preparation steps. I built a focused formatting tool to reduce repetitive manual work and make output more consistent.

entries.title: Portfolio Card Studio
entries.description: Generate consistent visual cards for showcasing projects.
solution: A large project portfolio needs visual consistency, but manually recreating layouts for every project wastes time. I built a dedicated card-generation tool around my portfolio's visual system so project graphics can be produced faster while retaining a consistent structure.

entries.title: Banner Studio
entries.description: A focused design utility for quickly generating consistent banners.
solution: Instead of repeatedly rebuilding layouts in a full design application, I created a dedicated interface for the banner-production workflow.

entries.title: Brand Aid
entries.description: A native macOS app for generating consistently branded graphics—base image, logo, crop, and placement in one pass.
problem: Every project on this site, and every social card announcing one, needed the same branding treatment: a base image, my logo placed consistently, cropped to the right ratio. Doing that by hand in a general design tool for dozens of images added repetitive setup work every time.
solution: I built Brand Aid, a native macOS app that takes a base image, overlays a logo at a configurable size and position, crops to a chosen aspect ratio, and exports it ready to use.
It's what generated most of the thumbnails across this project archive, including its own.
highlights: Used to produce this site's own thumbnails

entries.title: ProfileLauncher
entries.description: Launch the right browser environment for the right context.
solution: Multiple accounts and browser contexts create unnecessary friction when switching between different kinds of work. I built a lightweight launcher around those contexts so the correct environment can be opened directly.

entries.title: Custom Obsidian Planning System
entries.description: Projects, tasks, habits, meals, and events in one connected workspace.
problem: My projects, tasks, habits, meals, and events lived in separate views and mental models inside Obsidian, so planning meant switching between disconnected systems instead of working from one place.
solution: I extended Obsidian's Calendar and Bases plugins into a connected planning system: color-coded content types, the ability to add items directly from calendar dates, dedicated habit tracking and meal planning, and filtered database views across tasks, events, and projects.
The interface itself is the point—it's a customized system built around how I actually plan, not a generic template.

entries.title: Seamless DSLR-to-Server Photo Ingest
entries.tagline: FTP · EXIF Automation · Mac Mini Server
entries.description: An FTP pipeline that captures photos straight from my DSLR and automatically organizes them into folders on my home server.
problem: Getting photos off a DSLR and onto my server meant connecting a cable or card reader, then manually sorting the files—extra steps that added friction to something that should be instant.
Even AirDrop, while wireless, just dumps everything into one folder instead of organizing by shoot, date, or camera.
solution: I set up an FTP server on my Mac mini and configured my DSLR to upload directly over Wi-Fi the moment I take a photo.
Incoming photos are automatically picked up, organized into folders based on their metadata, and filed exactly where I want them—no cable, card reader, or AirDrop step required.
highlights: Runs on a home Mac mini server

entries.title: Cross-Device Automation System
entries.description: A personal automation ecosystem spanning Mac, iOS, and terminal environments. Unified Raycast scripts, Obsidian workflows, and shell aliases into a consistent, context-aware productivity layer that reduces friction across development, writing, and research tasks.

entries.title: Messaging Sticker Conversion
entries.description: A batch processing pipeline to extract, convert, and package messaging sticker assets across multiple formats and platforms, automating frame extraction, transparency normalization, and export to APNG/WebP formats compatible with LINE, WhatsApp, and Telegram.

entries.title: Proxy Phase — Project Lifecycle System
entries.description: Structured project phases that turn ambiguous work into actionable next steps.
problem: Projects change over time. Planning, active work, waiting, review, and completion require different kinds of attention.
Most basic project systems don't represent those transitions particularly well.
solution: I built Proxy Phase to introduce explicit lifecycle states into my project system.
Projects can move through structured phases, making their current state easier to understand and allowing other parts of the system to respond accordingly.

entries.title: WaniKani for Obsidian
entries.description: Japanese-learning progress and reviews integrated directly into Obsidian.
problem: Language-learning data often remains isolated inside individual learning platforms.
That creates unnecessary context switching and makes it harder to connect structured study with personal notes and knowledge.
solution: I built an integration between WaniKani and Obsidian so relevant learning information could become part of my existing study environment.

entries.title: Bunpro Reviews for Obsidian
entries.description: Reverse-engineered an undocumented integration to bring grammar reviews into Obsidian.
problem: I wanted Bunpro review information available inside my broader learning system, but the integration I needed wasn't exposed or documented in a way that supported what I wanted to build.
solution: Instead of abandoning the integration, I investigated how the service communicated and reverse-engineered the pieces necessary to build my own workflow.
I then connected that information with Obsidian so grammar study could become part of my existing learning environment.

entries.title: Proxy Policy — Rule-Based Automation
entries.description: A policy layer that defines how my productivity system should behave.
problem: As a productivity system becomes more automated, hard-coding every behavior creates complexity and makes workflows difficult to change.
solution: I developed Proxy Policy as a separate rules layer that lets system behavior be defined through policies rather than scattered across individual workflows.
This separates what the system should do from the individual tools responsible for doing it.

entries.title: Local-First Commonplace System
entries.description: Save once. Organize, preserve, and resurface information across devices.
problem: Interesting articles, highlights, social posts, and book passages become scattered across services and are often never seen again.
I wanted saved information to become part of a durable personal knowledge system rather than disappear into another read-later queue.
solution: I combined a customized fork of Omnivore with my Obsidian vault and custom TRMNL pipeline.
Saved articles and highlights can flow into my local knowledge environment, while selected information can later be resurfaced through an always-on e-ink display.
The system also provides a destination for Kindle highlights and other material I want to preserve.

entries.title: Proxy Study
entries.description: A Japanese study tool I rebuilt from scratch after the iOS app I relied on disappeared from the App Store.
problem: I paid for and relied on an iOS Japanese study app that was removed from the App Store, taking the tool I'd built a habit around with it.
solution: Rather than searching for a replacement, I'm rebuilding the app's core study experience myself, connected to the same broader productivity and knowledge system as my other Proxy tools.

entries.title: Resume Atelier
entries.tagline: Career Tools · Automation · Documents · Product Design
entries.description: A purpose-built workspace for creating and managing tailored resumes.
solution: Applying to different roles often means maintaining numerous versions of the same resume and repeatedly reorganizing overlapping experience. I built Resume Atelier as a dedicated environment for working with resume content and creating role-specific versions more efficiently.

entries.title: Kindle Screensaver Studio
entries.description: A purpose-built workflow for preparing custom Kindle screensaver artwork.
solution: Images created for ordinary screens aren't necessarily prepared correctly for an e-reader's dimensions and display characteristics. I built a focused tool around preparing artwork for the Kindle rather than repeatedly performing the same image-processing steps manually.

entries.title: AI Multilingual Learning System
entries.description: An AI-assisted pipeline that classifies vocabulary and grammar items, generates context-rich flashcard content, and turns it into study-ready Anki decks with less manual work.
solution: Finding a word takes seconds; creating a useful, well-formatted flashcard takes considerably longer. I built a pipeline that uses LLMs to classify vocabulary and grammar items and generate context-rich flashcard content, then pipes the structured output into Anki decks -- supporting English, Japanese, and Farsi learning tracks.

entries.title: Save Safari Tabs
entries.description: Preserve groups of browser tabs without leaving dozens of pages open.
solution: Browser tabs frequently become temporary bookmarks, task lists, and research queues. I built a focused workflow for saving those sessions so they can be closed without losing the context they represent.

entries.title: TimewBar
entries.description: Time tracking where I can see it without opening another application.
solution: Time tracking loses value when checking or updating it requires constantly opening another application. I built a lightweight interface designed to keep relevant tracking information accessible during everyday work.

entries.title: Video Notes
entries.description: A workflow for turning video consumption into usable notes.
solution: Useful information inside videos is difficult to reference later unless it becomes structured information somewhere else. I created a workflow around capturing video-related notes so important information can move from passive viewing into my broader knowledge system.

entries.title: Lulu Book Pipeline
entries.description: A repeatable production pipeline for preparing books for Lulu publishing.
problem: Publishing requires many small production steps that become repetitive across multiple revisions and books.
solution: I created a repeatable pipeline around my publishing workflow to reduce manual preparation and make revisions easier to manage.

entries.title: Cycle
entries.description: A single-key window switcher and app launcher, forked and rebuilt from an existing Alt-Tab replacement.
problem: The Alt-Tab replacement I liked required holding a modifier plus another key to switch windows, and had no way to search for a window or launch an app that wasn't already open.
solution: I forked the app and reworked it to trigger with a single key instead of a modifier combination, then added search: search finds an open window and switches to it directly, or if the app isn't open, shows it so I can launch it—one tool for switching and launching.

entries.title: Dash
entries.description: A dashboard for viewing all my custom apps and tools and confirming everything on the network is running correctly.
problem: With dozens of custom apps, plugins, and services running across my machines, there was no single place to see what existed or confirm everything was still healthy.
solution: I built Dash as a watcher and viewer for all of my custom apps and tools, so I can check on and maintain everything running across the network from one dashboard.

entries.title: Both Ears
entries.description: One-ear, mono, noisy, or quiet audio in — clean, hearable stereo out.
solution: A drag-drop utility that takes one-ear, mono, noisy, or quiet audio and produces clean stereo audio at a hearable volume, including fan-noise removal.

entries.title: RAM Watchdog
entries.description: A lightweight watchdog for keeping an eye on memory usage.
solution: System performance problems can develop gradually while the information needed to diagnose them remains buried inside system-monitoring tools. I built a lightweight menu-bar monitoring utility focused specifically on making RAM behavior easier to track, with pre-crash alerts and the ability to flush cache or quit/relaunch memory hogs directly.

entries.title: iMessage Backup Tool
entries.description: A custom workflow for preserving iMessage data outside the standard interface.
solution: Messaging applications are excellent for conversation but aren't necessarily designed around long-term archival workflows. I built tooling around extracting and preserving message information so it can be retained outside the normal conversation interface.

entries.title: iMessage Archive Viewer
entries.description: Browse archived conversations outside the original messaging application.
solution: Backing up information solves preservation, but the archive still needs to be usable. I created a dedicated viewer around the archived data so conversations can be browsed independently of the original application.

entries.title: iMessage Auto Reply
entries.description: Custom automation for responding to specific messaging workflows.
solution: I built a focused automation layer around iMessage to reduce repetitive manual responses where predetermined, per-person behavior makes sense.

entries.title: WGStatusBar
entries.description: WireGuard status and controls where they're immediately accessible.
solution: A background networking service can be working correctly while still providing poor visibility into its current state. I built a compact menu-bar status interface to make relevant WireGuard information and controls easier to access.

entries.title: Capture Bar
entries.description: A persistent capture surface for getting information into my system quickly.
solution: Capture workflows fail when recording something takes enough effort that you postpone it. I created a dedicated capture interface that keeps the entry point immediately accessible and connects it with the rest of my workflow.

entries.title: NAS Deployment
entries.description: Deployed and configured a NAS as the backbone of a network's storage, sharing, and self-hosting.
problem: The network needed a reliable, centralized place to store, back up, and serve files, photos, and self-hosted services instead of scattering them across individual machines.
solution: I deployed and configured a NAS as the storage and services backbone for the network -- the foundation that the backup, sharing, surveillance, and self-hosted app projects all run on.

entries.title: Smart Home System Design
entries.description: Designed and integrated a smart home system across devices and protocols.
solution: I designed and set up a smart home system, integrating devices across my home network into one connected setup.

entries.title: Multi-User NAS Backup Management
entries.description: Managing automated backups for multiple people's multiple devices across the home network.
problem: Photos and files live across many devices belonging to different people in the household, and losing any of it was a real risk without a consistent backup system.
solution: I set up and maintain NAS-based backup coverage for multiple people's multiple devices, making sure everything gets backed up automatically rather than relying on each person to do it themselves.

entries.title: WireGuard VPN for Remote NAS Access
entries.description: Built WireGuard VPN access into the network so the NAS and its services are reachable securely from anywhere.
problem: I wanted to reach my NAS and home services from outside the house without exposing them directly to the internet.
solution: I built WireGuard VPN access into my network, so I can connect securely from an external location and reach the NAS and other home services as if I were on the local network.
See also WGStatusBar, the menu-bar client I built for checking connection status at a glance.

entries.title: Cloudflare Tunnel File & Photo Sharing
entries.description: Connected NAS photo and file sharing to the outside world through a Cloudflare Tunnel, without exposing the NAS directly.
problem: I wanted to share photos and files from my NAS with other people without opening ports on my router or exposing the NAS directly to the internet.
solution: I connected the NAS's photo and file sharing systems through a Cloudflare Tunnel, so others can access shared content through a secure public link while the NAS itself stays off the open internet.

entries.title: Self-Hosted Community Platform
entries.description: Deployed Fluxer, a Discord-like community platform, self-hosted through the NAS.
solution: I deployed Fluxer, a self-hosted Discord-style community platform, running through my NAS infrastructure.

entries.title: Self-Hosted LMS Deployment
entries.description: Deployed a self-hosted learning management system through the NAS.
solution: I deployed a self-hosted LMS through my NAS infrastructure to run and manage online courses.

entries.title: Flarum Forum Deployment
entries.description: Deployed and self-host a Flarum discussion forum.
solution: I deployed a Flarum forum as a self-hosted discussion platform on my own infrastructure.

entries.title: WordPress Staging Environment
entries.description: Run and continually improve a WordPress staging site on a separate server from the NAS.
solution: I run and maintain a WordPress staging environment on its own server, separate from the NAS, using it to test and improve a live WordPress site before changes go live.

entries.title: Custom Firewall & Router (OPNsense)
entries.description: Installed and configured OPNsense as a custom firewall and router for the home network.
problem: A consumer router doesn't give the visibility or control needed to properly segment and secure a home network with many different devices and services.
solution: I installed and configured OPNsense as a dedicated firewall/router, giving me VLAN segmentation, custom firewall rules, and full control over how traffic moves through my network.

entries.title: Calibre RSS-to-Kindle News Delivery
entries.description: An internal network pipeline that pulls RSS news through Calibre and delivers it straight to Kindles.
solution: I built a pipeline where Calibre pulls news from RSS feeds and delivers formatted issues straight to Kindles over the internal network, with no manual syncing required.

entries.title: Self-Hosted NAS Surveillance System
entries.description: Home camera surveillance running through the NAS, with no subscription required.
problem: Most home security camera systems lock recording and viewing behind a monthly subscription.
solution: I run surveillance camera recording and monitoring through my NAS instead, avoiding subscription fees while keeping full control over the footage.

entries.title: Custom Desktop Builds for Clients
entries.description: Custom-built multiple desktop computers for clients.
solution: I've built multiple custom desktop computers for clients, selecting and assembling hardware suited to their specific needs.

entries.title: Vertical Crop
entries.description: Converts horizontal video to vertical video instantly — drag, drop, done.
problem: Client videos needed to go from horizontal to vertical format for social media, and reframing each clip by hand in a video editor was slow and repetitive.
solution: I built Vertical Crop, a drag-and-drop app that converts horizontal video to a centered vertical crop instantly -- no editor, no manual framing, just drop the file and get a ready-to-post vertical video.
This is the final iteration after two earlier versions refined the cropping approach.
highlights: Final iteration of an evolving tool

entries.title: Still Grabber
entries.description: Extracts a set number of still frames from a video, ready to use as social media thumbnails.
problem: Social media analysts needed still images pulled from video to use as post thumbnails, which meant manually scrubbing through footage and exporting frames one at a time.
solution: I built Still Grabber: set a number, drag and drop a video, and it extracts that many evenly-spaced still images automatically -- ready for a social media analyst to use directly as thumbnails.

entries.title: Pinnacle Thumbnail Maker
entries.tagline: Design Automation · Social Media · Client Branding
entries.description: A specific thumbnail-design tool for a client's social media, with saved layouts per post type.
problem: Different post types needed different thumbnail designs -- different text and colour placement -- and rebuilding each layout by hand every time was slow and inconsistent.
solution: I built a thumbnail-design tool specific to the client's social media, with layouts saved per post type.
Drop in a still image, paste in minimal text, and it produces an on-brand thumbnail matching that post type's design.

entries.title: Caption Pop
entries.description: Drag-and-drop video captioning powered by a local transcription model — no subscription required.
problem: Popular auto-captioning tools get near-perfect results but come as ongoing subscriptions, and even the good ones need occasional timing or text corrections.
solution: I built Caption Pop: drop in a video, and it connects to a local audio-transcription LLM to transcribe it and burn the captions directly onto the video.
Results are nearly perfect, and where they're not, the tool makes timing and text adjustments easy -- all without a recurring subscription.

entries.title: BGM Mixer
entries.description: Drag-and-drop background music mixing — random or chosen tracks added to video instantly.
problem: Adding background music to a batch of videos one at a time in an editor was slow when the music just needed to come from a standing set of approved tracks.
solution: I built BGM Mixer: drop in a video and a track is added from a pre-selected folder of audio, either chosen at random or picked specifically, giving instant background music without opening an editor.

entries.title: Pinnacle Photo Brander
entries.description: Adds a client's specific branding to photos for their social media.
solution: A simple app that applies the client's specific branding to photos before they go out on social media.

entries.title: Video Patch
entries.description: Covers a logo, caption, or burned-in text on video with a solid colour patch.
problem: A client had videos that needed part of the frame cut or hidden -- a logo, caption, or burned-in text that shouldn't be there -- without re-editing the whole video.
solution: I built Video Patch to do basic video touch-ups: it covers a logo, caption, or burned-in text with a solid colour patch, positioned and timed to exactly where it's needed.

entries.title: Still Motion
entries.description: Turns a photo into a vertical 1080×1920 video with slow motion and captions.
solution: I built Still Motion to turn a single photo into a vertical 1080×1920 video with slow Ken Burns-style motion and script-driven captions -- ready to post without opening a video editor.

entries.title: [Example] Accomplishment Placeholder
entries.description: Placeholder so the Accomplishment type filter has something to show. Swap this out for a real one (award, interview, speaking appearance, etc.) whenever ready.

entries.title: Nicholas Romich
entries.tagline: Senior Vice President of Product at CiraConnect · Managed Hamed directly
entries.description:
Hamed built communication programs that actually moved the needle. In a service industry where technology adoption directly affects how well teams serve our customer, that is not a common skill.

At CiraConnect, Hamed and I partnered on Communications and Education initiatives supporting our product teams. He managed several concurrent weekly and monthly campaigns reaching a team that grew from 800 to over 1,500 during his tenure, without losing quality across any of them. He produced a podcast series, launched an illustrated story series to engage our audience in formats most teams would not have the confidence to attempt, and led the design of responsive mass communication templates that reduced friction for our teams when messaging community owners at scale.

What made Hamed effective was not just output volume. He understood that when internal teams are better equipped to use technology, the customer they serve feel it directly. He closed that gap through consistent, creative campaigns across multiple formats, building the kind of adoption that actually changes how a team operates. If you need someone who can work across content strategy, internal communications, AI-assisted workflows, and product enablement with that end-to-end picture in mind, Hamed is that person. I would work with him again without hesitation.

entries.title: Edgar Sanchez
entries.tagline: Platform Engineer at CiraConnect · Worked with Hamed on different teams
entries.description:
I had the pleasure of working with Hamed during his time leading our internal communications program. What impressed me most wasn't just that he built our entire internal communications function from the ground up… it was how he did it.

Hamed has a rare gift for making the complex feel accessible. When we were rolling out new software and processes, he didn't just send out dry announcements. He used comics, storytelling, and creative content that actually made people want to engage with what could have been boring technical updates. His approach transformed our training programs and made adoption of our new Management/Board Portal smoother than anyone expected.

Beyond his professional skills, Hamed was genuinely a joy to work with. He brought enthusiasm and positivity to every interaction, always had a smile, and made collaboration feel effortless. We bonded over shared interests like home NAS setups, and his curiosity and passion for technology always came through in our conversations.

Hamed is professional, creative, and knows how to connect with people. Any team would be lucky to have him, and I'm confident he'll bring the same energy and innovation to whatever he tackles next.

entries.title: DJ Yoes
entries.tagline: Desktop Support Manager at RealManage · Worked with Hamed on different teams
entries.description:
I had the pleasure of working with Hamed at RealManage during a major software transition, and his clear, timely communications were a major reason it went so smoothly. He developed training materials, managed timelines, gathered feedback, and built our internal communications program from the ground up. By leveraging multiple channels (podcasts, newsletters, email campaigns, comics, and more), he kept our team -- and the wider audience -- up to date without ever resorting to jargon.

Hamed's creativity and initiative truly set him apart. He spearheaded internal CiraConnect podcasts, designed engaging visuals to explain new features, and crafted email announcements that people actually read. He partnered seamlessly with leadership, IT, design, and cybersecurity to align messaging with technical goals. Always reliable, detail-oriented, and ready to proofread or brainstorm, Hamed brings a powerful blend of strategic thinking and hands-on execution. Any organization would benefit from his expertise in change management, user engagement, and content strategy.

entries.title: Cheryl Veldman
entries.tagline: Account Manager at CiraConnect · Worked with Hamed on the same team
entries.excerpt: He was inventive in ways that none of us had ever dared to be in prior attempts at communicating about our work to our end users before he joined us: he created a podcast.
entries.description:
I have enjoyed working with Hamed. He joined our team at a critical time as we transitioned from one version of our proprietary software to an updated, but markedly different version. As we phased it in, a lot was going on, creating a material learning curve for our varied audiences. Our team was responsible for testing it, writing training material, responding to questions, and resolving bugs. There was a lot on the plates of a small team. He was responsible for communicating the progress and timelines, providing a forum for the training materials, taking in and responding to feedback, and generally keeping a broad audience up-to-date on the transition -- the actual test of how valuable that was came as we readied to retire the old site. We had a fair amount of anxiety about how the users would react, but it went smoothly. I genuinely believe Hamed's communications were critical in allowing for that success.

He was inventive in ways that none of us had ever dared to be in prior attempts at communicating about our work to our end users before he joined us: he created a podcast. He was also instrumental in composing a regular comic, so he was constantly working to reach out to all different audience types in whatever way they'd take it. He realized that we are not a "one-size-fits-all" audience. Of course, he also excelled at the "traditional" communication strategies of email blasts and announcements, making them eye-catching and readable. He created and maintained a support website as well.

I found him supportive and a kind team member who helped proofread and critique the work I was responsible for producing as part of our conversion and ongoing support. He takes the term "team" seriously.

entries.title: Timothy Crawford
entries.tagline: Account Manager at CiraConnect · Worked with Hamed on the same team
entries.description:
Hamed has talent, creativity and consistency. As part of our Business Empowerment and Solutions Team, he filled a vital gap between product development and informing the user base by creating all kinds of communications that went out to thousands of employees across the company. What impresses me most about Hamed is how quickly and accurately he was able to learn the things that he was supposed to communicate about. entries.title: Smart Subtitle Machine
entries.description: A subtitle translation pipeline that goes beyond literal text, using a per-series glossary and cultural context to keep translations faithful to tone, references, and idiom.
problem: Machine-translated subtitles read literally, but literal translation loses idiom, humor, and cultural references specific to the source language and the show itself.

A translator needs to stay consistent across an entire series -- the same character, joke, or honorific should translate the same way every time it appears, across hundreds of lines and many episodes.
Nobody can proof-watch every episode before it ships, so the pipeline itself has to catch its own errors instead of relying on a human to spot them after the fact.
solution: I built a subtitle pipeline that pairs local AI translation with a per-series "glossary brain" -- a locked reference of names, honorifics, and recurring phrases so translations stay consistent from episode to episode, with a scan step that flags new recurring names before they slip through unlocked.

Beyond literal translation, the pipeline considers cultural context: idioms, humor, dialect, and second-language dialogue get localized and register-matched rather than translated word-for-word, so a joke or turn of phrase lands the way it was intended for the target audience.

It extracts burned-in subtitles directly from video via frame-sampled OCR when no separate subtitle file exists, and transcribes dialogue locally when there's no source text to start from -- with speaker diarization run first so gendered, politeness-sensitive translation knows who's actually talking.

Before anything ships, an automated audit checks timing, line length, and reading speed, retimes cues to real speech onsets so subtitles never appear before the words, and a fidelity pass re-checks every uncertain line against the source -- every episode goes through the same gate, with no exceptions.
howItWorks: **Workflow:** Source video/audio/subtitles → OCR or local transcription → speaker diarization → glossary-aware translation → cultural/idiom pass → voice-activity-based retiming → automated mechanical audit → fidelity re-check → final subtitle file, muxed or burned into video
highlights: Per-series glossary "brain" locking names, honorifics, and recurring phrasing
Cultural, idiomatic, and dialect-aware localization, not literal translation
Burned-in subtitle extraction via frame-sampled OCR
Local speech transcription and speaker diarization, no cloud dependency
Voice-activity-based retiming so cues never appear before the words
Automated mechanical audit (timing, line length, reading speed) gating every delivery
Runs entirely on local AI models

entries.title: Song Translation & Publishing Pipeline
entries.tagline: Audio Translation · Video Production · YouTube Automation
entries.description: A pipeline that translates songs from one language to another and turns the result into a published video, from a raw audio file to a scheduled YouTube upload.
problem: Translating a song well takes more than swapping words -- meaning, rhythm, and emotional register all have to survive the move from one language to another, and recurring terms need to stay consistent across an entire body of work, not just one track.

Publishing translated music consistently means repeating the same manual steps -- transcription, translation, subtitle layout, thumbnail design, metadata writing, and scheduling -- for every track, and a mistake in any one of them (a wrong upload, a rights issue) isn't something you can quietly walk back.

Automating the SEO metadata (titles, descriptions, tags) is tempting, but a fully automated draft can get facts wrong in ways that matter -- publishing without a human check risks putting something inaccurate or tone-deaf into the description of someone else's work.
solution: Built on top of a broader subtitle-translation pipeline, this workflow takes a raw audio file and produces a finished, translated video ready to publish -- reusing the same transcription, locked-terminology glossary, and quality-audit tooling rather than duplicating it.
Multiple on-screen layouts are supported for pairing two languages at once (stacked, split, or vertical text), chosen to match the piece's tone and cadence.

A local LLM drafts SEO-oriented title, description, and tags directly from the actual translation, but every draft gets checked against the real translation and glossary before it's marked publish-ready -- a first draft got a factual relationship detail wrong in testing, which is exactly the kind of error the review step exists to catch.

The finished video connects to YouTube's Data API for a resumable, chunked upload with exponential backoff on server errors, a thumbnail generated from the source file's own cover art, and a paced schedule so releases go out on a steady cadence instead of all at once.

Two independent gates keep anything from publishing by accident: confirmed rights permission per track, and the channel owner's own one-time authentication setup -- both have to be true before a single upload call is allowed to run.
howItWorks: **Workflow:** Audio file → transcription → glossary-aware translation → multi-language subtitle layout → video assembly → LLM-drafted metadata (human-reviewed) → thumbnail generation → rights + auth gate check → resumable YouTube upload → scheduled release
highlights: Audio-to-video pipeline, no manual editing per track
Meaning- and rhythm-aware translation, not literal
Shared glossary system for consistent terminology across every track
Multiple on-screen subtitle layouts, including vertical text
Local LLM-drafted metadata, always human-reviewed before publishing
Resumable YouTube uploads with exponential backoff
Dry-run-by-default batch scheduling with per-item rights confirmation
Two independent safety gates (rights + auth) prevent accidental publishing

entries.title: Proxy Iconize
entries.tagline: Obsidian Plugin · Icon Packs · UI Customization
entries.description: An Obsidian plugin fork adding custom icon-pack support so files, folders, and menu items can carry their own recognizable icons throughout the vault.
problem: A large, actively-used vault is easier to navigate by sight than by reading every file name, but Obsidian's default file tree gives every note the same plain icon.
Existing icon plugins didn't support the specific icon packs and resolution behavior this vault needed.
solution: I forked and extended an Obsidian icon plugin to support additional icon packs and fix icon-resolution issues that appeared on a cold restart.
Files, folders, and specific menu items can now be assigned distinct icons, making the vault's structure recognizable at a glance.

entries.title: Proxy Hide
entries.tagline: Obsidian Plugin · Menu Cleanup · UI Customization
entries.description: An Obsidian plugin that removes duplicate and unwanted entries from context menus, keeping the right-click menu focused on what's actually useful.
problem: Installing several Obsidian plugins quickly clutters the right-click context menu with duplicate or rarely-used entries.
There wasn't a clean way to selectively hide specific menu items without disabling the plugins that added them.
solution: I built a plugin that patches Obsidian's menu system to selectively hide chosen context-menu entries, including duplicates introduced by other plugins.
Menu-patch ordering was tuned so the hide rules apply consistently regardless of what order plugins load in.
highlights: Removes duplicate menu entries from other plugins

entries.title: Children's Book
entries.tagline: Rhyme Writing · Trilingual Layout · Print Preview
entries.description: A writing and layout system for a rhyming children's book, built to compare three languages side by side and preview real printed page spreads before sending anything to press.
problem: Writing a rhyming children's book across three languages at once is hard to track by feel alone -- rhyme, rhythm, and meaning all have to line up on every page, in every language.
Some of the target languages read right-to-left, which flips not just the text but the entire page layout and spread order.
It's easy to approve a layout on screen that turns out wrong once it's actually printed and bound.
solution: I built an Obsidian-based writing system with columns for each language, laid out line by line so rhyme, rhythm, and meaning can be compared side by side as the text is written.
A local preview site renders actual page spreads for each language, including mirrored, right-to-left layouts for languages that need the whole spread flipped.
This let me proof rhyme and rhythm while writing, and proof the physical print layout before anything went to press.
highlights: Line-by-line rhyme and rhythm columns in Obsidian
Three languages compared side by side
Localhost preview of real page spreads
Automatic right-to-left mirrored layout for applicable languages

entries.title: Pinnacle Social Analytics
entries.description: An end-to-end pipeline connecting Google Drive, Google Sheets, and Notion with a series of custom apps that bulk-process client media and keep the asset manager and content calendar updated automatically.
problem: Client media moves through several distinct processing steps before it's ready to publish, and tracking what's been processed, where it lives, and what's scheduled next was manual and easy to lose track of.
Asset status and the content calendar were tracked separately from the tools doing the actual processing, so they constantly fell out of sync.
solution: I connected Google Drive, Google Sheets, and Notion with a set of custom-built apps that bulk-process media through each step of the pipeline, from raw upload through to finished, branded output.
As media moves through the pipeline, the Google Sheets asset manager and the Notion content calendar update automatically, so status always reflects what's actually been processed.
highlights: Bulk processing through a chain of custom apps
End-to-end tracking from raw media to publish-ready output
